summary: This memo defines managed objects corresponding to the parties, contexts, and access control policies of the SNMPv2 administrative model. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1447 describes where an SNMPv2 agent stores the things it needs to know about who is talking to it. It defines four tables: one for the parties, with their identity, address, passwords and clock; one for the contexts, which group the information a party is allowed to work with; one for the access rules between parties; and one for the views that say which parts of the management tree each context can see.

questions: what is an access control list in snmp
subtitle: Managed objects that describe the parties, contexts and access rules of the SNMPv2 administrative model.

tldr.problem: The SNMPv2 administrative model was defined as a set of properties: parties with authentication and privacy settings, contexts that group management information, and access control policies between them. Those properties needed a concrete form that an SNMP agent could hold and a manager could read and change.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines a MIB module with four tables. The party table holds each party's identity, transport address, authentication protocol, clock, keys and privacy settings; the context table groups information and points at a MIB view; the access control table says which subject party may do what to which target party; and the view table says which parts of the object identifier tree a context may see.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1447 is Historic and the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was an IAB standards track protocol when written, and the memo's Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed in it.

today: RFC 1447 is Historic, which means the RFC Editor recommends it for no further use. It was an IAB standards track protocol when written, defining the managed objects for the SNMPv2 administrative model of parties, contexts and access control, and it has not been obsoleted by a later RFC.

sections.title: What the Party MIB Is For
sections.content:
A network management system contains several, potentially many, nodes, each with a processing entity termed an agent which has access to management instrumentation; at least one management station; and a management protocol used to convey management information between the agents and the management stations. Operations of the protocol are carried out under an administrative framework which defines both authentication and authorization policies. Management stations execute management applications which monitor and control network elements, and network elements are devices such as hosts, routers and terminal servers, which are monitored and controlled through access to their management information.

Management information is viewed as a collection of managed objects residing in a virtual information store, the Management Information Base. Collections of related objects are defined in MIB modules, which are written using a subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One, termed the Structure of Management Information.

The Administrative Model for SNMPv2 defines the properties associated with SNMPv2 parties, SNMPv2 contexts and access control policies. It is the purpose of this memo, the Party MIB for SNMPv2, to define managed objects which correspond to these properties. For the purpose of exposition, the original Internet-standard Network Management Framework, as described in RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212, is termed the SNMP version 1 framework, and the current framework is termed the SNMP version 2 framework.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMPv2 had decided that a manager and an agent should identify each other, authenticate each other and have rules about who may see what. This memo is the part that puts those decisions into tables an agent can hold: parties, contexts, access rules and views.

sections.title: Textual Conventions and Administrative Assignments
sections.content:
The module defines several textual conventions, which are named types that carry a shared description. Party denotes an SNMPv2 party identifier, with syntax OBJECT IDENTIFIER; agents may impose implementation limits on the length of object identifiers used to identify parties, so a management station creating a party should be aware that an excessively long identifier may cause the agent to refuse the set operation and return an error such as noCreation. Context denotes an SNMPv2 context identifier with the same syntax and the same warning.

TAddress denotes a transport service address, with syntax OCTET STRING. For the snmpUDPDomain a TAddress is 6 octets long, the initial 4 octets containing the IP address in network byte order and the last 2 containing the UDP port in network byte order. Clock denotes a party's authentication clock, a non-negative integer incremented as specified or allowed by the party's authentication protocol; for noAuth it is unused and its value undefined, and for the MD5 authentication protocol it is a relative clock with 1-second granularity.

StorageType describes the memory realisation of a conceptual row: a row which is volatile is lost upon reboot, a row which is nonVolatile is backed up by stable storage, and a row which is permanent can neither be changed nor deleted. The defined values are other, volatile, nonVolatile and permanent.

The administrative assignments name the security protocols that may be used: noAuth, the protocol without authentication, noPriv, the protocol without privacy, desPrivProtocol, the DES privacy protocol, and v2md5AuthProtocol, the MD5 authentication protocol. Three temporal domains are also defined: currentTime, which refers to management information at the current time; restartTime, which refers to management information upon the next re-initialisation of the managed device; and cacheTime, which refers to management information that is cached and guaranteed to be at most N seconds old.

Finally, initialPartyId and initialContextId allocate a branch of the naming tree for use under stated conventions. When devices are installed they need to be configured with an initial set of SNMPv2 parties and contexts, which requires the assignment of several object identifiers, and any local network administration can obtain the delegated authority necessary to assign its own. The branch is provided for administrations that have not obtained that authority. The identifiers are called initial because they allow secure SNMPv2 communication to proceed, which in turn allows further parties to be configured through SNMPv2 itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo first fixes the types used throughout: what a party or context identifier is, what a transport address looks like, and how a row of a table is stored. It then names the pieces that the rest of the module refers to, including the four security protocols a party may use and the three kinds of time a reading can refer to.

sections.title: The SNMPv2 Party Database
sections.content:
The first of the four database groups is the SNMPv2 party database, a table of parties indexed by the party identifier. Each row holds locally held information about a particular party: the party identity, which uniquely identifies the party, and a party index, an integer between 1 and 65535 that must stay the same from one re-initialisation of the entity's management system to the next.

A row then describes how to reach the party and how to authenticate it. The party transport domain names the transport service, the party transport address gives the address in the form that domain requires, and the party maximum message size says how large a message may be. The party local flag says whether this entity is the party itself.

Authentication is described by the party authentication protocol, the party authentication clock, the party authentication private key and public key, and the party authentication lifetime, which bounds how long an authentication key may be used before it must be changed. Privacy is described in the same shape: a privacy protocol, a privacy private key and a privacy public key. The party clone from field records the party a row was cloned from, so that several parties can share settings without repeating them.

Each row also carries a storage type, saying whether the information is lost on reboot, kept in stable storage, or permanent, and a row status, the usual mechanism for creating, modifying and deleting rows under SNMP.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row of the party table describes one participant: who it is, where to reach it, how big a message it will accept, which authentication protocol it uses, the clock it counts with, its private and public keys, how long those keys are good for, and whether its traffic is private as well as authenticated. A row can also point at another row it was cloned from, so a group of parties can share one set of keys.

sections.title: The Contexts and Access Control Databases
sections.content:
The second group is the SNMPv2 contexts database. Each row holds locally held information about a context: the context identity, which uniquely identifies it, a context index with the same range and stability rules as the party index, a context local flag saying whether this entity realises the context, a context view index pointing at the MIB view the context may use, and a context local entity giving the entity this context refers to.

Three more fields give the context its place in time and in the proxy relationship. The context local time names the temporal domain the context refers to, one of the three defined by the module. The context proxy destination party and context proxy source party name the parties that stand in for this one when it proxies for them, and the context proxy context names the context used on the far side of that proxying.

The third group is the SNMPv2 access privileges database. Each row holds the access privileges for a particular subject SNMPv2 party when asking a particular target SNMPv2 party to access a particular SNMPv2 context. The row is indexed by the target, the subject and the resources, each of which is an integer between 1 and 65535. The target identifies the party that is the target of the policy and has the same value as the instance of the party index for that party, and the subject identifies the party that is the subject of the policy in the same way. The resources field identifies the set of resources the privileges apply to, and the privileges field holds the access privileges themselves, such as read and write.
sections.plainLanguage: A context is a named grouping of management information, and it points at a view saying which parts of the tree it covers. A context can also stand in for another party, which is how proxying is expressed. The access table then ties the three together: for a given target party, a given subject party and a given set of resources, it records what the subject is allowed to do.

sections.title: MIB Views
sections.content:
The fourth group is the MIB view database, holding locally held information about the MIB views known to an SNMPv2 entity. Each SNMPv2 context which is locally accessible has a single MIB view, defined by two collections of view subtrees, the included view subtrees and the excluded view subtrees, and every such subtree, included or excluded, is defined in the view table.

The rule for deciding whether an object instance is in a particular MIB view is stated precisely. Compare the object instance's object identifier with each of the MIB view's entries in the table. If none match, the object instance is not in the view. If one or more match, the instance is included in or excluded from the view according to the value of viewType in the entry whose value of viewSubtree has the most sub-identifiers. If multiple entries match and have the same number of sub-identifiers, the lexicographically greatest instance of viewType determines the inclusion or exclusion.

An object instance matches an entry when the number of sub-identifiers in it is at least as many as in the entry's viewSubtree, and each sub-identifier in viewSubtree matches its corresponding sub-identifier. Two sub-identifiers match either if the corresponding bit of viewMask is zero, the wild card value, or if they are equal. This wild card capability leads to the term a family of view subtrees, meaning the set of subtrees defined by a particular combination of values of viewSubtree and viewMask; where no wild card is defined, the family reduces to a single view subtree.

Each row of the view table holds the view index, which identifies the MIB view and must stay constant across re-initialisations, the view subtree, an object identifier naming the branch of the tree, the view mask, a bit mask of up to 16 octets that says which sub-identifiers must match and which are wild cards, and the view type, which is included or excluded. Implementations must not restrict the number of families of view subtrees for a given MIB view, except as dictated by resource constraints on the overall number of entries in the table.
sections.plainLanguage: A view says which parts of the management tree a context may see. It does that with a list of entries, each naming a branch of the tree and saying whether that branch is included or excluded. Each entry also carries a mask, so a single entry can cover a family of nearby branches rather than one. When entries overlap, the most specific one wins, and a tie is settled by the lexicographically greatest type value.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo has a Security Considerations section, and its entire content is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo.

Nothing in the document explains the authentication or privacy protocols it names, nor how the keys it stores should be protected. What the document does set out is the shape of the configuration an agent must hold: which protocol a party uses, the clock it counts with, the lifetime of an authentication key, and the private and public keys for both authentication and privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security. Its Security Considerations section says only that security issues are not discussed, so nothing in it should be read as advice on how to protect the keys it asks an agent to store.

viz.caption: THE FOUR TABLES OF THE PARTY MIB
WHAT ONE ROW OF THE PARTY TABLE HOLDS

items.title: Identity
items.text: partyIdentity and partyIndex, which must stay the same across a restart.

items.title: Transport
items.text: The transport domain, the transport address, and the maximum message size.

items.title: Authentication
items.text: The authentication protocol, the clock, and the lifetime of the authentication key.

items.title: Keys
items.text: The private and public keys used for authentication and for privacy.

items.title: Privacy
items.text: The privacy protocol that protects the traffic once authenticated.

items.title: Cloning
items.text: The party this row was cloned from, so several parties can share settings.

items.title: Storage
items.text: Whether the row is lost on reboot, backed up, or permanent.

viz.caption: THE TWO KINDS OF VIEW SUBTREE

items.label: included
items.desc: Objects under this subtree are part of the MIB view.

items.label: excluded
items.desc: Objects under this subtree are not part of the MIB view.
